extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, literary critics, and aspiring writers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing and managing narrative point of view in novels — balancing omniscient/pictorial narration and dramatic/scene-based methods, when to use first person, and how to 'dramatize' the narrator so the book feels self-contained and authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the mind and the eye objective (authenticate point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the omniscient author’s knowledge is unaccounted for it creates an 'inconclusive look'—the narrator’s mind and eye must be made objective, i.e. recognizable and verifiable within the book, so the story is equally wrought on every side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book must 'bring its own recognisances' because there is no external authority to vouch for it; otherwise one side may seem left 'in the rough'. Examples: contrast Vanity Fair (author conspicuous) with methods that include the narrator in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator—make the narrator a fact in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the act of recollection or the observing consciousness as a piece of action—a drama within the book—so the narrator’s activity authenticates and enhances the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calling up recollections can be presented as an enactment; this 'drama of the narrator' both authenticates the picture and adds independent interest. Example: Esmond (Thackeray) places the seer among the people he sees, giving measurable line of sight to characters like Beatrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person to give precision and individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute a characterized 'I' for the loose, general 'I' of the author to delimit a field of vision, supply a definite edge to the picture, and add personal colour to tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration provides a known, named viewpoint through which the reader sees; it supplies precision and a salience the abstract omniscient narrator lacks. Examples: Esmond, Copperfield, Harry Richmond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve dramatic scenes—hoard drama for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is 'the novelist’s highest light' and should be used economically; overuse diminishes its force and wastes its impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The economical procedure is to 'hoard' scenes, reserving them for moments of emphasis and climax (e.g., Bovary); using scenes prodigally lessens their force where essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pictorial (panoramic) and dramatic (scenic) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must manage both picture and drama: how to guide the story into the scene and how to pick it out of the scene — the quality of a novelist appears in this management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most novelists show a preference but use both; the best work 'imposes one method upon another' to correct weaknesses of each and retain advantages of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsupported authorial information (don’t 'show your hand' unnecessarily)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that openly comes straight from the author, which the reader cannot test, rests on weak authority and lessens the picture’s weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turgenev's habit of drawing the reader aside to pour information 'straight from Turgenev himself' is criticized: such intrusions make the picture less authoritative because they repose upon nothing the reader can verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose narration method to suit the subject (match method to subject’s needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick pictorial/omniscient or first-person/autobiographical narration according to what the subject requires: wide panoramas favour a pictorial method; portraits of inner growth may demand dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thackeray’s panorama needs a detached spectator; Copperfield’s long glance suits first-person memory; Meredith’s Harry Richmond needs a method that allows the narrator himself to be the subject. Match the method to whether the book’s subject is the spectacle or the narrator’s inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reporting wide sweep of life, rely on pictorial travelling glance
rubrics_metrics.description: To cover large spans and multiplicity of experience, a novelist will often need the pictorial method — a travelling glance that can sweep many facts summarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pictorial method enables coverage of breadth that dramatic scene cannot; yet it risks inserting a conspicuous author unless balanced by dramatizing devices (e.g., Flaubert blending his vision with Emma’s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend authorial vision unobtrusively with a character’s vision
rubrics_metrics.description: When using pictorial narration, blend the author’s acuter vision with a character’s point of view so the intervention is unobtrusive and the character’s vision appears to govern the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert does this with Emma Bovary—authorial intervention is so subtle the reader feels Emma’s point of view governs; this avoids the problem of an unaccountable omniscient seer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person to provide unity for episodic or rambling material
rubrics_metrics.description: An autobiographical 'I' can compose of its own accord: by belonging to one man, disparate events gain an indefeasible unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autobiography tolerates formlessness as charm; first-person reporting can draw a fragmentary tale together and stamp it as a single whole. Example: Harry Richmond (adventurous saga) and David Copperfield (long retrospective glance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of first-person when the narrator must himself be the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book’s primary aim is a searching, elaborate portrait of its narrator, the narrator’s retrospective reporting may be insufficient to show inner change; such inner history requires dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meredith’s Harry is expected to be both reporter and fully visible subject — an impossible demand if left to mere report. The narrator’s consciousness should be dramatized so the reader can 'get behind' the report and judge for themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator’s position measurable (naming and situating the seer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing who the seer is and where they stand (the 'line of sight') gives characters a new dimension and sharper relief; it prevents the subject from floating 'from anywhere, from nowhere'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Esmond’s clear situating of the seer makes Beatrix more solid than Becky in Vanity Fair, where the narrator’s location is unspecified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize memory when giving general accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a general account of many things or inner knowledge must be presented, render the remembering process itself as action so it explains its relation to the framed story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the reflective mind’s effort as dramatic action ('a play within a play') so the reader sees the recorder as part of the effect, not just an external reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading first-person narrators with tasks they cannot perform
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect a first-person narrator both to supply a panoramic pictorial view and to present a vividly dramatized inner life of equal force; pick which function is primary or provide additional dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harry Richmond is an example where the narrator is asked to be both vivid reporter and fully dramatized subject; when the latter is required, the method of autobiography may need to be surrendered or supplemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to enact central, essential affairs rather than merely describe them
rubrics_metrics.description: For the crucial matters of the story—changes of character, pivotal emotional events—prefer enactment (scenic drama) over mere pictorial report to achieve intensity and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'central, essential, paramount affair' should be dramatized; otherwise something is lost if it is represented solely by the hero’s account. Reserve scenes for such purposes rather than allowing continuous narration to dilute impact.
